intelligence.def: The ability to learn from experience, solve problems and use knowledge to adapt to new situations.

g-factor.def: General intelligence (g): a broad mental ability, proposed by Spearman, that underlies performance on many different kinds of tests, which is why their scores correlate.

multiple-intelligences.def: The view that intelligence is several distinct abilities rather than one general ability. Popular theories of this kind (such as Gardner's) have limited evidence that the abilities are truly separate.

mental-age.def: The level of performance typical of children of a given age, used on early intelligence tests. A child who does as well as typical 10-year-olds has a mental age of 10.

iq.def: Intelligence quotient. Originally mental age divided by chronological age, times 100. Modern tests compare a score with others of the same age on a normal curve with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.

standardization.def: Giving a test in the same way to everyone and setting norms from a large, representative sample, so individual scores can be compared with them.

reliability.def: The consistency of a test's scores: the same person scores about the same on two occasions (test-retest reliability) or on the two halves of the test (split-half reliability).

validity.def: How well a test measures or predicts what it is meant to. Construct validity: it measures the intended trait. Predictive validity: its scores predict a later outcome, such as grades.

stereotype-threat.def: A drop in performance when people fear confirming a negative stereotype about their group. Early studies found large effects; later, larger studies suggest the effect is smaller and less consistent.

stereotype-lift.def: A small rise in performance when people are reminded of a negative stereotype about a different group they are compared with.

flynn.def: The Flynn effect: the rise in average intelligence test scores across generations during the 20th century, too fast to be genetic. It has stalled or reversed in some countries.

group-variation.def: Within-group variation is the spread of scores inside one group; between-group variation is the difference between groups' averages. A trait can be strongly heritable within groups while a gap between groups is caused by the environment.

achievement-test.def: A test of what a person has already learned, such as a final exam.

aptitude-test.def: A test designed to predict a person's future performance or capacity to learn.

growth-mindset.def: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others.

fixed-mindset.def: The belief that abilities are fixed and cannot be changed much by effort.
